verses.text: Now while Ezra prayed and made confession, weeping and casting himself down before God’s house, there was gathered together to him out of Israel a very great assembly of men and women and children; for the people wept very bitterly.

Shecaniah the son of Jehiel, one of the sons of Elam, answered Ezra, “We have trespassed against our God, and have married foreign women of the peoples of the land. Yet now there is hope for Israel concerning this thing.

Now therefore let us make a covenant with our God to put away all the wives, and those who as are born of them, according to the counsel of my lord, and of those who tremble at the commandment of our God. Let it be done according to the law.
Arise; for the matter belongs to you, and we are with you. Be courageous, and do it.”
Then Ezra arose, and made the chiefs of the priests, the Levites, and all Israel, to swear that they would do according to this word. So they swore.

Then Ezra rose up from before God’s house, and went into the room of Jehohanan the son of Eliashib. When he came there, he ate no bread, nor drank water; for he mourned because of their trespass of the captivity.
They made a proclamation throughout Judah and Jerusalem to all the children of the captivity, that they should gather themselves together to Jerusalem;

and that whoever didn’t come within three days, according to the counsel of the princes and the elders, all his possessions should be forfeited, and himself separated from the assembly of the captivity.

Then all the men of Judah and Benjamin gathered themselves together to Jerusalem within the three days. It was the ninth month, on the twentieth day of the month; and all the people sat in the wide place in front of God’s house, trembling because of this matter, and because of the great rain.
Ezra the priest stood up and said to them, “You have trespassed, and have married foreign women, to increase the guilt of Israel.
Now therefore make confession to Yahweh, the God of your fathers, and do his pleasure; and separate yourselves from the peoples of the land, and from the foreign women.”
Then all the assembly answered with a loud voice, “As you have said concerning us, so must we do.
But the people are many, and it is a time of much rain, and we are not able to stand outside. This is not a work of one day or two, for we have greatly transgressed in this matter.

Now let our princes be appointed for all the assembly, and let all those who are in our cities who have married foreign women come at appointed times, and with them the elders of every city, and its judges, until the fierce wrath of our God is turned from us, until this matter is resolved.”
Only Jonathan the son of Asahel and Jahzeiah the son of Tikvah stood up against this; and Meshullam and Shabbethai the Levite helped them.

The children of the captivity did so. Ezra the priest, with certain heads of fathers’ households, after their fathers’ houses, and all of them by their names, were set apart; and they sat down in the first day of the tenth month to examine the matter.
They finished with all the men who had married foreign women by the first day of the first month.
Among the sons of the priests there were found who had married foreign women: of the sons of Jeshua, the son of Jozadak, and his brothers, Maaseiah, and Eliezer, and Jarib, and Gedaliah.
They gave their hand that they would put away their wives; and being guilty, they offered a ram of the flock for their guilt.
Of the sons of Immer: Hanani and Zebadiah.
Of the sons of Harim: Maaseiah, and Elijah, and Shemaiah, and Jehiel, and Uzziah.
Of the sons of Pashhur: Elioenai, Maaseiah, Ishmael, Nethanel, Jozabad, and Elasah.
Of the Levites: Jozabad, and Shimei, and Kelaiah (also called Kelita), Pethahiah, Judah, and Eliezer.
Of the singers: Eliashib. Of the porters: Shallum, and Telem, and Uri.
Of Israel: Of the sons of Parosh: Ramiah, and Izziah, and Malchijah, and Mijamin, and Eleazar, and Malchijah, and Benaiah.
Of the sons of Elam: Mattaniah, Zechariah, and Jehiel, and Abdi, and Jeremoth, and Elijah.
Of the sons of Zattu: Elioenai, Eliashib, Mattaniah, and Jeremoth, and Zabad, and Aziza.
Of the sons of Bebai: Jehohanan, Hananiah, Zabbai, Athlai.
Of the sons of Bani: Meshullam, Malluch, and Adaiah, Jashub, and Sheal, Jeremoth.
Of the sons of Pahathmoab: Adna, and Chelal, Benaiah, Maaseiah, Mattaniah, Bezalel, and Binnui, and Manasseh.
Of the sons of Harim: Eliezer, Isshijah, Malchijah, Shemaiah, Shimeon,
Benjamin, Malluch, Shemariah.
Of the sons of Hashum: Mattenai, Mattattah, Zabad, Eliphelet, Jeremai, Manasseh, Shimei.
Of the sons of Bani: Maadai, Amram, and Uel,
Benaiah, Bedeiah, Cheluhi,
Vaniah, Meremoth, Eliashib,
Mattaniah, Mattenai, and Jaasu,
and Bani, and Binnui, Shimei,
and Shelemiah, and Nathan, and Adaiah,
Machnadebai, Shashai, Sharai,
Azarel, and Shelemiah, Shemariah,
Shallum, Amariah, Joseph.
Of the sons of Nebo: Jeiel, Mattithiah, Zabad, Zebina, Iddo, and Joel, Benaiah.
All these had taken foreign wives; and some of them had wives by whom they had children.

footnotes.content: Ezra's broken prayer drew the people—not because he was eloquent, but because his weeping was honest. The Lord draws near to those who confess truly. Even leaders must sometimes fall to their knees first.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Shecaniah speaks up with the hardest words: we have sinned. But notice—he names hope too. The courage to name what went wrong is the first step toward repair and toward Jesus, who restores what seemed lost.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A covenant to obey God's law sounds severe, but it was born from love—love for the God they had forgotten, and for the people He had preserved. Real repentance reshapes how we live and whom we bind ourselves to.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Shecaniah offers Ezra what he needed most: the people's resolve to stand with him. A leader's burden grows light when others say 'we are with you.' This is how the Lord upholds us—often through the shoulders of those beside us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: An oath sworn before God binds a people together. Ezra called for it not to shame, but to weave accountability into their hearts—so they would remember this turning, this choice, this covenant moment.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ezra could not eat or drink. His fasting wasn't theater—it was the weight of a people's sin resting on him until it was made right. Sometimes leaders carry the grief that opens the way for healing.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The proclamation reaches all the captives—scattered across the land, everyone must gather. A true turning involves the whole people, not just the willing few. The Lord calls us all to the work of repentance.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Three days was the boundary. The consequence was severe, but it was also just: those who refused to gather were making a choice. The Lord's law calls us to choose, and choice matters.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They gathered trembling in the rain—frightened, cold, wet. Yet they came. The ninth month, the twentieth day: exact. And notice—the raw weather didn't stop them. Fear of the Lord ran deeper than comfort.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ezra didn't soften the truth. 'You have trespassed.' No excuse, no varnish. The hardest mercy sometimes looks like a priest willing to name the sin plainly, trusting that the people can bear it and turn.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Confession and separation walk together. The people are asked to make it public, to name their broken covenant before God and the assembly. That honesty, though costly, is how we return to wholeness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: One voice, loud and clear: we will do as you have said. Unity in repentance is rare and beautiful. The people chose to bear the weight of their own correction—not because Ezra forced them, but because they owned the sin.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The people are honest about the difficulty. The work is heavy, the weather harsh, and the transgression wide. True repentance doesn't pretend the path will be easy—it simply commits to walk it anyway.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They set up a system: princes, elders, judges in each city, all to hold one another accountable. Restoration requires structure and witnesses. The Lord works through order and community, not through shame alone.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A few stepped back from the covenant. Jonathan, Jahzeiah, and the others—their names are kept. Even in Scripture, dissent is named. The people of God are not always perfectly united, yet the work goes on.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The investigation began on the first day of the tenth month. Systematic, careful, each person named. This wasn't hasty judgment but patient, witnessed accounting. The Lord's justice is neither quick nor careless.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Three months of work—the investigation finished by the first day of the first month. They gave themselves the time it needed. Healing a people's covenant takes seasons, not moments. Patience is its own form of obedience.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The priests led in confessing. Those who teach the law must first own their own breaking of it. No one stands apart. The high and the humble fall alike—and all must rise together.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They gave their hand—a pledge—and they offered a ram. Confession alone wasn't enough; they made restitution before God. True turning includes both the word and the cost of change.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Hanani and Zebadiah—the sons of Immer. Each name matters to the Lord. In His sight, every person's breaking and every person's turning is known and counted.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The sons of Harim, five men named. The roll of those who confessed spreads through the city. Each one had to choose, face themselves, and step forward to be counted among the turned.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The sons of Pashhur, six named. Each family, each household, each man—the catalog is precise. The Lord's record of repentance is not vague; He knows the heart of each person who turns.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Levites and singers too. Those set apart for service were also caught in the same sin. No office shields us from our own breaking; all must confess and be healed by the Lord's grace.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The singers, the porters—every role in the temple's life touches this turning. Even the gatekeepers and musicians had to decide: will I turn with the people, or will I hold back?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The sons of Parosh, seven men. Among Israel the turning spreads—family after family, clan after clan. One confession builds courage in the next. The Lord's work moves through a people's collective willingness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The sons of Elam, six named. Shecaniah was the son of Jehiel of Elam—the man who first spoke courage to Ezra. His own household rose to the work too. True leaders turn first, then their own families follow.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The sons of Zattu, six. The list continues, each name a person who had to face the mirror, confess, and begin again. The Lord's restoration comes one name at a time, yet it shapes a whole people.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The sons of Bebai, four men. The catalog lengthens. In this genealogy of turning, we see not shame but honesty—the willingness of Israel to face what they had done and to be counted as repentant.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The sons of Bani, six names. Each person's turning is witnessed. Nothing is hidden from the Lord—and here, nothing is hidden from the people either. Transparency is part of how a community heals.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The sons of Pahathmoab, seven men. The households grow, the names accumulate. Each person was more than a name to the Lord—He knew the shape of their life, the battles they faced, the grace that would hold them.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The sons of Harim, beginning their list. Notice how the same family names appear again—Harim is mentioned before, and here we see more of their kin. The Lord calls families, not just individuals, to wholeness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Benjamin, Malluch, Shemariah. The sons of Harim continue their confession. The Lord sees no one as too small, too overlooked, or too late to turn. Every name in His book is precious.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The sons of Hashum, seven men. The catalog continues through Israel like a river of turning. Each name is proof that grace meets the person who confesses—not tomorrow, but today, here, known.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The sons of Bani begin their list again. More households, more families stepping into the light. The work of repentance ripples: one turning makes space for the next turning to happen.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Benaiah, Bedeiah, Cheluhi. Small names, ordinary men—yet they mattered enough that their choice to confess was written down. The Lord forgets no one who turns toward Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Vaniah, Meremoth, Eliashib. The sons of Bani. Scripture names them all. It's a long list because repentance, when true, is thick and wide—it reaches into every corner of a people's life.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Mattaniah, Mattenai, Jaasu. Three more. The list is the point—not as punishment, but as record. The Lord keeps a book of those who confess and turn. It's a kind book, a good book.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Bani, Binnui, Shimei. The names continue their way through the family of Bani. In listing them, Scripture honors them—not as failures, but as people who had the courage to be seen returning.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Shelemiah, Nathan, Adaiah. More sons of Bani. Each one faced the same choice: hide and hope, or confess and turn. They chose to be counted. The Lord honors that kind of courage.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Machnadebai, Shashai, Sharai. Three more into the light. The catalog spreads across Israel like dawn breaking through a dark night—each name a person, each person a choice, each choice a turning.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Azarel, Shelemiah, Shemariah. The end of Bani's sons draws near. They are written in a book of turning, not of shame. The Lord makes a record not of our failure, but of our return.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Shallum, Amariah, Joseph—the last of Bani's house. Three final names before the last family. The roll call ends not with judgment, but with names. Each one was seen, known, and accepted as turned.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The sons of Nebo, six men. This is the final household. The last names are no less important than the first—Jeiel, Mattithiah, Zabad, and the others stand equally in the Lord's sight, equally turned, equally restored.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo in this stark ending: all these men had taken foreign wives, and some had children. The Lord doesn't erase the cost of our sin—He faces it. Yet He calls us to the harder, braver road: to confess it all, bear the cost, and be made whole through repentance. As of 2026-10, we still know that courage.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
